'''Paul James Chirik''' (born June 13, 1973) is an American [[chemist]] known for his work in sustainable chemistry using Earth-abundant metals like iron, cobalt, and nickel to surpass the performance of more exotic elements traditionally used in [[catalysis]]. He is the Edwards S. Sanford Professor of Chemistry and chair of the chemistry department at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Paul Chirik Named Chair of Princeton Chemistry |url=https://chemistry.princeton.edu/news/paul-chirik-named-chair-of-princeton-chemistry/ |website=Princeton University Department of Chemistry |access-date=21 July 2023}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
Chirik received his B.S. in chemistry from [[Virginia Tech]],<ref name="vita">{{cite web |title=Paul Chirik |url=https://chirik.princeton.edu/paul-chirik/ |website=Chirik Group Princeton University, Dept. of Chemistry |access-date=21 July 2023}}</ref> studying [[organometallic chemistry]] under the advisement of Joseph Merola. He earned his Ph.D. in 2000 at the [[California Institute of Technology]] studying polymerization and hydrometallation chemistry with [[John E. Bercaw]].
After his postdoctoral work at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], Chirik joined the chemistry faculty at [[Cornell University]] until 2011, when he was named the Edwards S. Sanford Professor of Chemistry<ref name="vita" /> at Princeton University.

== Research ==
Chirik’s multidisciplinary research seeks to transform traditional catalysis, which relies on exotic metals like platinum and rhodium to drive chemical reactions. Instead, Chirik uses alternative, Earth-abundant metals like iron and cobalt, developing techniques that allow these metals to mimic or surpass the performance of exotics.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rosner |first1=Hillary |title=A Chemist Comes Very Close to a Midas Touch |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/10/16/science/modern-day-alchemy-has-iron-working-like-platinum.html |access-date=21 July 2023 |work=New York Times |date=15 October 2012}}</ref>
An important example of this research was published in 2021 in ''Nature Chemistry'',<ref>{{cite journal |title=Iron-catalysed synthesis and chemical recycling of telechelic 1,3-enchained oligocyclobutanes |last1=Beromi |first1=Megan Mohadjer |last2=Kennedy |first2=C. Rose |last3=Younker |first3=Jarod M. |last4=Carpenter |first4=Alex E. |last5=Mattler |first5=Sarah J. |last6=Throckmorton |first6=Joseph A. |last7=Chirik |first7=Paul J. |journal=Nature Chemistry |date=25 January 2021 |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=156–162 |doi=10.1038/s41557-020-00614-w |pmid=33495607 |pmc=7875253 |bibcode=2021NatCh..13..156M }}</ref> in which Chirik detailed a route to recyclable plastics through a molecule he discovered called oligocyclobutane.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Plump |first1=Wendy |title=Chirik discovers "transformative" route to recyclable plastics |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2021/01/25/chirik-discovers-transformative-route-recyclable-plastics |website=Princeton University |access-date=21 July 2023}}</ref> This molecule can be “unzipped” back to its original monomer by employing an iron catalyst in a process known as [[depolymerization]].

Another major focus of Chirik’s lab is improving the process surrounding iron- and cobalt-based catalysis cross-coupling for carbon-carbon bond formation,<ref>{{cite web |title=Iron and Cobalt Catalysts for Cross Coupling|url=https://chirik.princeton.edu/research/iron-and-cobalt-catalysts-for-cross-coupling/ |website=Chirik Group Princeton University, Dept. of Chemistry |access-date=21 July 2023}}</ref> an essential technology used by the pharmaceutical industry to develop new therapies. Chirik publishes regularly on this technology, with recent papers on cobalt-catalyzed cross-coupling<ref>{{cite journal |title=Cobalt-Catalyzed C(sp2)–C(sp3) Suzuki–Miyaura Cross-Coupling Enabled by Well-Defined Precatalysts with L,X-Type Ligands |last1=Mills |first1=L. Reginald |last2=Gygi |first2=David |last3=Ludwig |first3=Jacob R. |last4=Simmons |first4=Eric M. |last5=Wisniewski |first5=Steven R. |last6=Kim |first6=Junho |last7=Chirik |first7=Paul J. |journal=ACS Catalysis |date=20 January 2022 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=1905–1918 |doi=10.1021/acscatal.1c05586 |pmid=36034100 |pmc=9400687 }}</ref> and the addition of halides to a reduced-iron pincer complex to create an improved pathway for a desired end product.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Oxidative Addition of Aryl and Alkyl Halides to a Reduced Iron Pincer Complex |last1=Rummelt |first1=Stephan M. |last2=Peterson |first2=Paul O. |last3=Zhong |first3=Hongyu |last4=Chirik |first4=Paul J. |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=8 April 2021 |volume=143 |issue=15 |pages=5928–5936 |doi=10.1021/jacs.1c01486 |pmid=33829769 |pmc=8293301 |bibcode=2021JAChS.143.5928R }}</ref>

In 2022, Chirik was among the first chemists in the nation<ref>{{cite web |last1=Plump |first1=Wendy |title=Princeton's Paul Chirik awarded $1M for green chemistry research |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2022/07/21/princetons-paul-chirik-awarded-1m-green-chemistry-research |website=Princeton University |access-date=21 July 2023}}</ref> to receive a [[Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation]] exploration-phase grant in [[green chemistry]] based on his proposal for iron catalysts for a biorenewable hydrocarbon future.<ref>{{cite web |title=Grant Detail |url=https://www.moore.org/grant-detail?grantId=GBMF11394 |website=Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation |access-date=22 July 2023}}</ref>

He has been the editor-in-chief of the journal ''Organometallics'' since 2015.<ref name="editor">{{cite web |title=About the Journal |url=https://pubs.acs.org/page/orgnd7/about.html |website=ACS Publications |access-date=22 July 2023}}</ref>
